tweets.text: RT @ethvisionorg: Several issues exist: 1. The statement that "if the staked ETH exceeds a certain threshold, such as 50%, it will create a strong incentive for the remaining 50% to stake to avoid dilution" is unfounded; it's only one possibility. In reality, as the staking ratio increases, the staking yield gradually decreases. The current surge in staking is largely due to the prolonged low price of ETH (which is also just one factor). The staking ratio is a complex factor, not a simple 0 or 1 model. 2. The statement that "holding a high proportion of $ETH staked will introduce many problems and act as a centralized force" is also unfounded. LSTs' value is entirely rooted in ETH. If ETH is decentralized, then LSTs are unlikely to become a centralized force. Because if LSTs try to undermine ETH, they will perish simultaneously. 3. The statement that "LSTs with a large ETH staking ratio will introduce tail risk because they become too big to fail. In the event of a major leak, the chain may be forced to fork" sounds correct, but strictly speaking... Any project/DApp that grows large will face the same risks. Even Ethereum's own code may have bugs. Presuming LSTs guilty based on theoretical possibilities demonstrates ignorance of law and common sense. 4. Vitalik and his core group have long been wary of LSTs like Lido because LSTs are not an unexpected bonus of the free market designed by EF. Those around Vitalik are deeply concerned that the growing influence of LSTs will weaken their own, so they are attempting to "reduce power" by addressing top-level rules. This is a typical power struggle, not a purely technical issue. In reality, L2s pose a much greater threat to Ethereum, and Vitalik, due to his deep involvement in L2s design, only acknowledged the problem this year. 5. My view is that Ethereum's current monetary policy and issuance curve do not have real problems. LSTs are a spontaneous market outcome and are part of Ethereum's greatness. Trying to change a problem that isn't a problem is itself a problem. Ethereum is already a massive economy worth hundreds of billions of dollars; the stability of its monetary policy is a prerequisite for its long-term consensus building. The large number of left-wing individuals within Ethereum (EF) excels in philosophy and theory but lacks substantial practical experience and product development mindset. This poses a threat to Ethereum to some extent, and the very proposal of this EIP exposes this problem. The near-universal opposition to this absurd proposal from the community also serves as a check and balance. Ethereum remains great, but not because of a few individuals. Ethereum doesn't need heroes; some should voluntarily step aside.

The scanners move at machine speed. Responsible disclosure is still hunting around for an email address. @OpenSats stepped up and gave the effort a home. Code RED will prioritize support for red-teaming critical Bitcoin software and reimburse past LLM token costs. The dedicated Red Team Fund is live. This week exposed how cheap vulnerability discovery has become and how unprepared most open-source projects are to receive the results. If your code touches bitcoin, publish a security contact. If you can reproduce and triage findings, the Red Team needs you.

tweets.text: To All Crypto Bros: Crypto Has a Ticking Clock Problem, and Almost Nobody in Finance is Talking About It (Especially SEC Chairman Paul Atkins) Two things happened in the last two weeks that should be on every financial professional’s radar (and should be of serious concern for all crypto HODLers, especially bitcoin HODLers): 1️⃣ IBM CEO @ArvindKrishna told @jimcramer that within 3-4 years, we should all be “rather paranoid” about quantum computing’s threat to the cryptography underpinning crypto. Cramer is reportedly selling his Bitcoin in response (linked below). 2️⃣ Duke’s @leereiners published a comprehensive article in Duke's FinReg Blog arguing -- a must read -- that financial regulators need a plan for quantum-vulnerable digital assets, because right now, they don’t have one (linked below). The Quantum Fear. Meanwhile, quantum-vulnerable blockchain infrastructure is being integrated deeper into the traditional financial system every month: spot ETFs, bank custody, stablecoin legislation. The trend line is hard to dismiss. Research published this year cut the estimated quantum hardware needed to break current cryptographic keys by an order of magnitude. Millions of bitcoin especially reside in older, exposed and vulnerable wallet formats. The industry insists it will upgrade before the threat materializes. But to execute a coordinated cryptographic migration across every chain, wallet and custodian is unprecedented. Y2K Bug, Deja Vu All Over Again? Make no mistake about it -- this is no Y2K bug-like situation. I should know because I experienced the Y2K bug crisis firsthand. I worked at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) during the Y2K bug threat and actually stood guard in the SEC Enforcement ticker room that night at 11:59 PM when the clock turned. All went fine (thankfully) but only because the SEC spent all of 1998 and 1999 fiercely enforcing Y2K Bug disclosure from, and Y2K Bug remediation by, all SEC-registered entities, especially brokerage firms, clearing firms and national exchanges. Specifically, the SEC strictly enforced Year 2000 (Y2K) disclosures by requiring registered firms to report their readiness and remediation progress. The SEC also initiated historic crackdowns and levied civil penalties against brokerage firms and investment advisers that failed to file or filed incomplete Y2K compliance forms. The SEC efforts were massive and extraordinarily effective -- just look at this Y2K Bug Report (one of many) from those days: https://t.co/ZMlJyUlMvt For example, to enforce Y2K readiness across the financial sector, the SEC instituted mandatory reporting rules and released comprehensive interpretative guidance, such as: -- Staff Legal Bulletin No. 5: The SEC issued and subsequently updated this bulletin to compel public issuers and registered investment companies to disclose material impacts the Y2K problem could have on their businesses. This included remediation costs, untimeliness risks, and third-party failures. -- Form BD-Y2K & Form TA-Y2K: Broker-dealers and transfer agents were legally required to submit disclosure reports detailing their readiness. Firms not deemed fully compliant by the late summer of 1999 were threatened with mandatory cessation of business operations. The SEC also famously took aggressive, sweeping enforcement actions against firms that missed statutory filing deadlines or failed to submit complete assessments: -- Broker-Dealer Crackdowns: In late 1998, the SEC charged 37 brokerage firms for failing to file or fully complete Part II of Form BD-Y2K. Nineteen of these firms initially agreed to settle, paying civil penalties ranging from $5,000 to $25,000. -- Investment Advisers & Transfer Agents: In the summer of 1999, the SEC brought enforcement actions against investment advisers and transfer agents (e.g., Peachtree Stock Transfer, Amervest) for missing deadlines or submitting incomplete updated TA-Y2K forms. Penalties reached upwards of $22,500 per firm, alongside cease-and-desist orders and formal censures. Following extensive internal efforts, the SEC also imposed a moratorium from June 1, 1999, to March 31, 2000, on any new rulemakings requiring major computer reprogramming by Commission-regulated entities to allow firms to focus strictly on Y2K remediation. Today's SEC and Quantum. Sadly, don’t expect the cavalry to ride in from the SEC. @SECPaulSAtkins spent years before his appointment on the other side of the table: co-chair of the Token Alliance, the crypto lobby’s advocacy arm; consultant to digital asset firms through his firm, whose client list included FTX, massing up to $6 million in crypto-related holdings disclosed at his nomination. @SECPaulSAtkins is no watchdog. He is the industry’s own man, installed in the regulator’s chair. And he has governed exactly as expected: “Project Crypto,” declaring most digital assets aren’t securities at all and swapping enforcement for accommodation, all while the quantum clock ticks. In short, when the Y2K Bug arose as an issue, the SEC spoke loudly and often, acted swiftly and aggressively and fully mobilized. Fast forward to today and the Quantum threat, there's only radio silence from the SEC and gleeful abandon from @SECPaulSAtkins. Does Big Crypto Even Care About the Quantum Threat? Let’s be honest about who’s guarding the vault. This is an industry born in shadow and raised on anonymity, whose track record runs from collapsed exchanges to vaporized stablecoins to founders sitting in federal prison. Their answer to the quantum threat is ‘trust us—we’ll upgrade in time.’ Trust? From a den of thieves whose entire history is one long exercise in separating holders from their money. The only thing new here is that quantum computing might beat them to it. The Stark Reality: Asking this SEC to plan for the day crypto’s cryptography cracks is asking a man to blow the whistle on the Big Crypto industry that made him. The chances are slim and none (and Slim just left town). Fail not at your peril crypto bros. Start asking questions now. . . . And though you may not agree with my views on crypto -- my take is that crypto's only use is for criminals -- you should still heed my admonition (and please don't kill the messenger).
